subject: POC follow-up: tokenization, stop behavior, streaming semantics

Subject: Quick recap + a few questions before POC kickoff

Thanks again for the call earlier — good alignment on scope. Before we sign off for the internal OKs and schedule the POC kickoff, the engineering team asked for a short clarification on three areas so we can size the work: 

1) Chat vs completions behavior: for a guided chat flow (system + user turns) do you recommend using the chat API or the completions endpoint with a stitched prompt? Any differences in token accounting and stop handling we should expect?

2) Tokenization / max_tokens / stop: we saw different docs mentioning token limits per request and per response — what's the recommended way to make sure our autocomplete stops reliably (we have domain-specific stop tokens plus streaming)? Also curious how streaming interacts with stop sequences.

3) Streaming semantics + SDK: when we enable streaming in the SDK what guarantees do we get about order/partial-final tokens and the use of function/tool calling mid-stream? Are streaming chunks guaranteed to be incremental prefixes or can they be batched out of order?

If you can reply to these 3 points with concrete examples, we can finalize the internal tech brief and get our infra folks scheduled.

Thanks,
Arya
Senior Staff Engineer, Lumen Health

Hi Arya — thanks for the clear list. Below are concise answers and a few suggested defaults for the POC. Forwarding technical notes to Ben and Karthik for any runtime / infra add-ons.

1) Chat vs completions
- Recommendation: use the chat API for multi-turn conversational flows. The chat API natively models roles (system, user, assistant) and supports function/tool calling and structured output semantics.
- Token accounting: both endpoints count tokens similarly (input + output). The chat endpoint includes role metadata which affects tokenization slightly, but there is no different per-token billing model — billing is on tokens consumed.
- When would you use completions? If you have a single-shot prompt where you assemble everything server-side (and want to reuse legacy code), completions is fine. For safety/tool-calling/structured responses, prefer chat.

2) Tokenization / max_tokens / stop
- max_tokens: this parameter controls the maximum number of tokens in the model's reply. Set conservatively for the POC (we recommend 256-512 for short assistant replies).
- Stop sequences: you can provide up to several stop tokens (strings). For the chat API, a stop sequence is applied to the assistant output stream; the runtime will truncate the output when a stop is emitted.
- Streaming + stop: when streaming is enabled, the runtime will stop emitting further chunks once a stop sequence is detected. Clients should treat the final chunk as possibly truncated at the stop boundary. In practice: you may see the stop token appear at the end of the last chunk rather than as a separate chunk.
- Tokenization note: use our tokenizer utility in the SDK to precompute token counts for prompts (helps you ensure prompt + max_tokens stays within model limits). We'll include a short helper in the runbook.

3) Streaming semantics + SDK behavior
- Streaming is delivered as ordered incremental deltas (SSE/websocket style). Chunks are incremental prefixes of the final assistant text; chunks are delivered in order and you will not receive tokens out of order.
- Function/tool calling: if the model triggers a function call, the stream will emit a "function_call" event (in order) followed by the function arguments payload. If the tool is invoked server-side, you'll see an assistant role switch with the function name and args.
- Partial vs final: the SDK surfaces a boolean flag on the last chunk ("done": true) so you can distinguish partial vs final. For the POC, plan for reassembly logic that concatenates chunks and applies the stop filters on the reassembled text.

Additional POC guidance (practical):
- Default configuration: chat endpoint, streaming enabled, max_tokens=512, stop=["\n\n--END--", "\nUser:"] for deterministic cutoffs.
- Auth: standard API key (Bearer). For Private deployments we support mTLS and integration with customer KMS — we can surface details if you plan to host in VPC.
- Routing: set the model param (e.g., "redwood-llm-xl") and region; our default router pins by region then model capability. If you need a hard constraint (latency-sensitive), send routing hints in the request header (we'll share the header key in the runbook).
- Embeddings / reranker: embeddings endpoint returns float vectors and an id; for reranking we recommend deriving candidate embeddings server-side and using our similarity search helper (we'll include an example in the runbook).

I'll attach a short runbook with recommended SDK snippets and stop presets for your domain. If it looks good, let's lock the POC kickoff for next Wed.

Best,
Tessa Morgan
Director, Solutions — Redwood Inference

Adding two runtime notes from infra: 
- Continuous batching + KV cache: for multi-turns with large context, enable KV cache to avoid re-encoding previous tokens each turn — this reduces latency and token cost. We'll enable this on the dedicated POC pool.
- Max sequence & truncation: if you plan to send long transcripts, we recommend truncating the oldest user messages server-side rather than relying on the model to ignore them. Our SDK has a sliding-window helper (see runbook).

I'll also attach a small text file with example stop presets we use internally that map to common UI behaviors.

—Ben
Principal Engineer, Runtime
